title: Batch Packer
hints: The answer is a number between two easy bounds. What are they?
If someone hands you a capacity, can you check in one pass whether b batches are enough? Is feasibility monotone in the capacity?
Binary search the capacity between max(len) and sum(len). The check packs greedily, starting a new batch only when the next sequence would overflow.

wrong.average_cap.cpp: answers max(longest, ceil(total / b)), ignoring that batches must be consecutive
wrong.low_zero.cpp: starts the search at 0 instead of the longest sequence, so a too-small capacity is accepted
wrong.tle_linear_cap.cpp: tries every capacity upward one by one (fails the perf group)

strategy.question: Scout the statement: which plan fits n up to 2*10^5, lengths up to 10^9 and 'minimise the largest consecutive-batch sum'?
options: DP over (batches used, sequences placed), trying every last cut
Binary search the largest-batch cost; check each guess greedily in one pass
Sort the lengths and deal them round-robin into b batches
Take ceil(total / b), the perfect average
strategy.why: The DP is O(b n^2), far too slow. Feasibility of a cost cap is monotone and checkable by a greedy O(n) pass, so binary search gives O(n log(sum)). Sorting breaks the required order, and the average is only a lower bound: consecutive batches rarely split evenly.
